text: Under the law, Israel was nepios: an infant ruled by guardians. In Christ you've had your coming-of-age as a full son.
explanation:
"The heir, as long as he is a child, does not differ at all from a slave, though he is master of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father." The word for child, nepios, means an infant or minor. Rules like "Don't touch the knives" are right for toddlers, but insulting to adults. The law was a paidagogos, a child-minder, "until Christ came."

Then God sent His Son "to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption as sons": huiothesia, son-placement, the ceremony where a father declares his child a grown son and heir. Galatians isn't describing gradual growth; it's your status. "You are no longer a slave but a son."

text: God promised Abraham he'd be "heir of the world." Heirs of that promise can't be always sick and always broke.
explanation:
"The promise that he would be the heir of the world was not to Abraham or to his seed through the law, but through the righteousness of faith." The word for world, kosmos, speaks of an ordered, beautiful arrangement, with its riches and influence. And "if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise."

It's hard to inherit the world flat on your back. Healing and provision are lesser blessings, all included in the greater one. So why do so many believers live without them? "If those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise made of no effect." The inheritance comes through the righteousness of faith, never by trying harder at the law.

text: Because Abraham didn't withhold his son, God had covenant ground to give His own.
explanation:
God gave Adam dominion, and Adam handed it to Satan. God couldn't simply snatch it back; He had to do it righteously. So He cut a covenant with a man, Abraham. But could a mortal man keep his side? The test came on Mount Moriah. Abraham raised the knife over Isaac, and God stopped him: "Now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son."

In a covenant, what one partner gives, the other gives too. Abraham's willingness opened the way, legally and righteously, for God to give His own Son. "He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?"

text: Teach your child identity, not just rules: "You're a Jesus boy. A Jesus boy tells the truth."
explanation:
People ask how we'll raise moral children without drilling them in the Ten Commandments. Most adults who insist on them can't even recite them. Yet small children can easily learn John 3:16. There's grace there.

Instead of "Thou shalt not," speak to who they are: "You're a Jesus boy. A Jesus boy doesn't lie. A Jesus boy protects others; he doesn't bully them." Behaviour flows from identity. "Be imitators of God as dear children." Children who know they're dearly loved naturally want to be like their Father.

text: In Revelation, only the redeemed address God as "You." The angels speak of Him in the third person.
explanation:
The twenty-four elders sing, "You are worthy… for You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood… and have made us kings and priests." No angel could sing that; angels were never redeemed. When the myriads of angels join in, the song shifts: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain." Heaven has order, and closest to the throne are the redeemed.

So don't come to God as a servant hovering at a distance. "You did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry out, 'Abba, Father.'" The Spirit of truth can't bear witness to a lie, and approaching as a slave is one. Come close; He longs to hear your voice.

text: The shepherd's rod is for wolves. The crook on his staff is for sheep that fall.
explanation:
"Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." Some teach that a shepherd breaks the leg of a lamb that keeps wandering, then carries it until it learns. You won't find that in Psalm 23: no "He breaks my legs." In Israel the rod was a weapon against lions and wolves, or thrown ahead of a sheep to turn it from a ravine, never to beat it.

And the staff has a crook at the end precisely because the shepherd expects his sheep to stumble. When you fall, He doesn't strike you; He hooks you gently and lifts you back. That's why His rod and staff are a comfort, not a threat.

text: "Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, be loosed?" Once you believe, you qualify.
explanation:
A woman had been bent double for eighteen years. Jesus laid hands on her, and she stood straight; the first face she saw was His. The synagogue ruler complained, "There are six days on which men ought to work." His "ought" was about labour. Jesus answered with a different "ought": "Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound… be loosed from this bond?"

Not everyone in that synagogue was a child of Abraham in that sense. When she believed in Jesus, she became one, and from that moment, Jesus couldn't leave her bound a minute longer. He said the same of Zacchaeus: "Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham." If you believe, so are you.
